questions.q: According to the lesson, what fundamentally distinguishes a machine learning model from traditional software?
options: Its behavior is learned statistically from data rather than written as explicit rules by a person
It runs on a different kind of computer hardware
It cannot be deployed over the internet
It always requires more storage space than any traditional program
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that a model's logic is learned from data, not authored as explicit, readable rules.

questions.q: Which three consequences does the lesson say follow from AI being 'learned, not authored'?
options: Scale, opacity, and inherited risk
Lower cost, faster hiring, and smaller teams
Better documentation, clearer code, and easier debugging
Reduced need for data entirely
questions.explain: The lesson names scale, opacity, and inherited risk as the direct consequences of learned (rather than authored) logic.

questions.q: Per the lesson, who ends up accountable when a deployed model makes a bad decision?
options: The organization that deployed the model and acted on its output
No one, since models are not legally attributable to any party
Only the original model vendor, in every case
The end customer who was affected
questions.explain: The lesson argues that "the vendor's model did it" rarely holds up — the deploying organization is accountable to customers and regulators.

questions.q: What does the lesson say ungoverned AI failure typically looks like in practice?
options: A quiet pattern, like underperformance for one group going unnoticed for months
A single dramatic company-wide outage
An immediate and obvious crash of the entire system
A visible public announcement from the AI vendor
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that the risk is usually quiet and compounding, not one dramatic event.

questions.q: What is 'model drift,' as introduced in this lesson?
options: A model's real-world performance degrading as conditions change after deployment
The physical movement of a server between data centers
A planned, intentional update to a model's code
The time it takes to train a model from scratch
questions.explain: The lesson defines model drift as performance degrading over time as real-world conditions shift, to be covered in depth later in Chapter 4.
